description: To develop the understanding of advanced algorithms. To study the complexity of advanced algorithms. To design new algorithms or modify existing ones for new applications and analyze their space & time efficiency.

syllabus.title: Introduction
syllabus.body: Models of computation, randomized polynomial identity testing algorithm (Schwartz-Zippel), Karger's randomized min-cut algorithm, randomized primality testing, Markov's and Chebyshev's inequality, moment generating functions and Chernoff bounds, randomized routing.

syllabus.title: Moments and Deviations
syllabus.body: Second-moment method, numerical probabilistic algorithms, Lovász local lemma with applications, Poissonization technique, power of two choices, metric embeddings.

syllabus.title: Markov Chains and Martingales
syllabus.body: Intro to Markov chains, mixing times, strong stationary times, and coupling; martingales, stopping times, the martingale stopping theorem and applications.

syllabus.title: Approximation Algorithms
syllabus.body: Greedy approximation algorithms, dynamic programming and weakly polynomial-time algorithms, linear programming relaxations, randomized rounding, load balancing.

outcomes: Apply basic concepts of approximation, randomization and distributed computing in algorithmic context.
Design randomized parallel, approximation and distributed algorithms that run fast or return correct output with high probability.
Derive good upper bounds for the expected running time of advanced algorithms.
Apply the probabilistic method to show the existence of certain combinatorial objects.
textbooks: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms, Third Edition, MIT Press and PHI, 2010.
Rajeev Motwani, Prabhakar Raghavan, Randomized Algorithms, Cambridge University Press, 2014.
Mitzenmacher and Upfal, Probability and Computing: Randomized Algorithms and Probabilistic Analysis, Cambridge University Press, 2nd edition, 2017.
